entries.summary: Today we are releasing DuckDB 2.0.1, the first patch release of our 2.0 LTS line. This release ships bugfixes, performance improvements, and security patches.
entries.text: Today we're releasing DuckDB 2.0.1, the first patch release in the 2.0 LTS (Cyanoptera) line. This planned release arrives one month after 2.0.0 and contains bugfixes, performance improvements, and security patches. In addition, it provides a more convenient way of registering custom extension repositories. You can obtain a copy from the installation page. For a detailed overview of the changes, see the release notes on GitHub. Read on for some highlights. Changes That May Require Action A few fixes in this release change existing behavior. In each case, the previous behavior was incorrect or a security risk, so we chose to fix it in 2.0.1 rather than wait for the next major release. If you rely on any of the behaviors below, review them before upgrading. Stricter SECRET Scope Matching A SECRET scoped to a host or bucket could also match other hosts or buckets with the same prefix, so it could be sent somewhere it wasn't meant for (#28684). A URL now matches such a scope only if it is identical to the scope or continues with a /. For example, the scope s3://bucket- no longer matches s3://bucket-1/. Action: check your host- and bucket-scoped SECRETs and make sure each scope uses the full host or bucket name. If a URL has an explicit port, the scope must include it too. UPDATE ... FROM and MERGE Again Apply Every Match In DuckDB 2.0.0, if several source rows matched the same target row, MERGE raised an error and UPDATE ... entries.summary: On 11 November 2026, the DuckDB User Group held its first workshop in Amsterdam, together with Hugging Face. Pratik Patel from Hugging Face led the session.
entries.text: In one afternoon, attendees built a pipeline that finds the products with falling ratings in 2.1 million Amazon reviews and explains why. DuckDB did the filtering and an LLM summarized the complaints. At the end, each attendee had a Hugging Face Space that they can call as an API. What We Built The data was the appliances part of the Amazon Reviews 2023 dataset. That is 2.1 million reviews and about 1.2 GB of raw JSON lines. Nobody downloaded it over the venue Wi-Fi. Attendees built and tested everything on their laptops with a 22 MB sample. Then the same two files ran on Hugging Face against the full data. The afternoon had five modules. Build locally. An ingest script converted the sample from JSON lines into two Parquet tables, one for reviews and one for products. It runs in seconds, so attendees could change a column and run it again. Find the trouble. A file of DuckDB queries, run with duckdb < sql/analysis.sql, showed the rating distribution, followed one product month by month, ranked products by how much their rating fell in the last six months, and selected the most helpful recent 1 and 2 star reviews for one product. Run it on the full data. The same ingest script ran as a Hugging Face Job on all 2.1 million reviews. The job read the data inside the Hugging Face network and wrote the Parquet files to a Storage Bucket. The hardware costs $0.01 an hour, and the job ran during the coffee break. Build the workflow. entries.summary: From interactive maps to graph exploration, DuckDB makes it possible to analyze data without a database server.
entries.text: Quote You should own your data. It can live on your computer, not everything has to live in the Cloud. It can be synced via the cloud, but you decide when to keep it local and when not. Ilya Boyandin, creator of SQLRooms Ilya Boyandin is a software engineer, the creator of SQLRooms, FlowmapBlue, and Flowmap City. He worked on geospatial data analytics at Unfolded, the company founded by the team behind the open-source data visualization projects deck.gl and kepler.gl, which was later acquired by Foursquare. How DuckDB Entered the Picture Ilya first used DuckDB in Flowmap City, a side project for visualizing mobility flows that he still maintains. Working with a small budget, Ilya wanted to keep Flowmap City easy to operate with minimal infrastructure. DuckDB’s WebAssembly build lets the app run analytical queries in the user’s browser without a database server. Uploaded datasets are stored as Parquet files in S3. When someone opens a project, the app loads the data into DuckDB-Wasm through presigned URLs. As users pan, zoom, or change filters in Flowmap City, DuckDB-Wasm runs SQL queries in the browser to update the map. A single interaction can trigger a number of queries preparing the data for the current viewport: Ilya explains: “We can now do much of the analysis and visualization in the browser. This keeps infrastructure requirements low and can be faster because queries don’t need a round trip to the server.” From a Side Project to SQLRooms Much of Flowmap City’s data-l
entries.title: Local Analytics Doesn’t Need a Database Server

entries.summary: DuckDB is fast among other reasons because it stores data by column, so a query reads only the columns it names.
entries.text: Why Columns? DuckDB stores each column separately instead of storing each row as one record. A query that touches three columns out of fifty reads only those three. That design choice explains many of DuckDB’s performance features. Columnar storage compresses well because a column holds values of one type, and those values often repeat. The engine processes each column in vectors of 2,048 values at a time. And a query that asks for fewer columns does less work. The examples in this post use a sample dataset of 400 ducks, each marked with a numbered leg band (a ring) and seen at one of four ponds between October 2025 and April 2026. The sightings table has five columns: ring_id, pond, species, weight_g, and seen_at. SELECT * FROM sightings LIMIT 3; ┌─────────┬───────┬─────────┬──────────┬─────────────────────┐ │ ring_id │ pond │ species │ weight_g │ seen_at │ ├─────────┼───────┼─────────┼──────────┼─────────────────────┤ │ R0001 │ south │ wigeon │ 862 │ 2025-11-06 12:18:38 │ │ R0002 │ south │ wigeon │ 578 │ 2025-12-04 00:12:54 │ │ R0003 │ south │ wigeon │ 734 │ 2026-01-06 16:50:41 │ └─────────┴───────┴─────────┴──────────┴─────────────────────┘ Every example runs in the DuckDB CLI or from Python with duckdb.sql(...). pip install duckdb # Python curl https://install.duckdb.org | bash # CLI Querying Files in Place You don’t need to load data before you query it. DuckDB treats a file path as a table and infers column names and types from the file. SELECT * FROM 'ponds.csv'; ┌────

entries.summary: JetBrains users had long asked to join data across different database connections in a single query.
entries.text: When JetBrains set out to let developers join data across different database connections in a single query, it chose not to build its own cross-database query engine. Instead, DataGrip, its database IDE, embeds DuckDB to execute those queries, and exposes DuckDB’s SQL dialect directly to the developers writing them. Quote DuckDB turned out to be the simplest option to integrate. Ilia Epelbaum, DataGrip, JetBrains Querying across Data Sources DataGrip is JetBrains’ IDE for working with databases and writing SQL, developed since 2015. The same database functionality is also available as a plugin inside the other JetBrains IDEs, so the feature reaches well beyond DataGrip itself. For a long time, users had been asking for one thing in particular: the ability to run a single query across more than one data source. The most common request was to join data from different database connections in one query. DataGrip could already execute queries against each connection, but nothing tied the results together, so the team needed an engine that could. Choosing DuckDB over Building Its Own JetBrains explored several approaches. It considered Apache Calcite, handling the queries itself using PSI (Program Structure Interface, the internal code representation JetBrains uses across its IDEs), and DuckDB. DuckDB won on ease of integration. “DuckDB turned out to be the simplest option to integrate,” says Ilia Epelbaum, who works on the DataGrip team. The deciding feature was the ability to reg
entries.title: How JetBrains Built Cross-Database Queries into DataGrip with DuckDB

entries.summary: After years building kdb+-based data platforms for banks and hedge funds, Ryan Hamilton wanted an analytical engine he could recommend to smaller teams without specialized infrastructure or expensive licensing.
entries.text: Quote I like the simplicity of just a small thing running and working. And then you can get more complex. Ryan Hamilton, founder, TimeStored Fifteen Years of Heavyweight Infrastructure For about fifteen years, Ryan Hamilton has built large market-data platforms for banks and hedge funds. Most of that work was in kdb+, integrated with real-time messaging systems such as Solace. He built much of the platform at UBS and almost all of it at Citi, contributed to Morgan Stanley's, and most recently worked at a hedge fund. His users are typically teams of 10 to 15 quants. They are deep specialists in finance who spend anywhere from a tenth to more than half their time on technology. Ryan's job has been to store their data efficiently so they can get on with their work. Sometimes he leads a team to do that. Sometimes he builds it himself. Sometimes he talks quants out of building infrastructure on their own. Problems That Didn't Need a Heavyweight Answer Alongside that work, startups, smaller tech firms, and smaller funds kept asking Ryan the same question: what should we run this on? For years he had no good answer. He tried other systems but found that their license was prohibitively expensive, their setup didn't offer an embedded mode of operation, or they were much more operationally involved than he wanted at the time. entries.title: Bringing Local Analytics to the Quant's Desktop

entries.summary: After nearly two decades working with increasingly sophisticated data infrastructure, data engineer [Matt Martin](https://www.linkedin.com/in/mattmartin14/) discovered DuckDB could handle many of the analytical tasks…
entries.text: Quote There actually is something out there that's easy to use and doesn't require a bunch of infrastructure overhead. Matt Martin From Copy-Paste to Code Matt's career started in 2008 the way many data careers do: with spreadsheets. As a fresh graduate, he spent his days copying and pasting between Excel, Microsoft Access, and SQL Server. Assembling a single report could take three hours, and one mistake meant starting over. “There's got to be an easier way,” he remembers thinking. His dad taught him how to write VBA macros, and that was the first step. Next, he got access to the SQL Server and Oracle databases behind those spreadsheets and started querying the source directly instead of other people's workbooks. Macros turned into scheduled stored procedures, and stored procedures turned into automated pipelines. When he started, the team published its 20 to 30 daily reports by 10 AM. By the time he had automated the process, the reports were out by 6 AM, before anyone had touched anything. Teradata, BigQuery, and the Spark Years From there, Matt moved into big data. Teradata gave him his first taste of massively parallel processing, along with lessons about data skew and distributing work evenly across nodes. Around 2016, at The Home Depot, he moved to Google BigQuery. BigQuery did not support stored procedures at the time, so Matt picked up Python, then pandas and eventually Apache Spark. entries.summary: We released DuckDB 2.0.0 last week with an improved Quack protocol and `VARIANT` support, asynchronous I/O, and many other features.
entries.text: Last week we released DuckDB 2.0.0 LTS, our biggest feature release so far. The announcement covered the headline items: the Quack protocol, asynchronous I/O, the first-class VARIANT type, agent mode, the PEG parser, and triggers. DuckDB 2.0.0 is now available in all primary clients – check the installation page for instructions on installing or upgrading. A release of this size ships many smaller improvements that never make it into the original announcement. In this post, we highlight a few of these gems. To find the documentation for everything that is new in 2.0, see the “What's New in the Docs for 2.0” page. Python Appender Inserting rows one at a time is inefficient, and building up a giant INSERT statement is awkward. Therefore, the preferred solution for inserting large amounts of data has been the appender. However, it was only available in some clients (C/C++, Go, Java, etc.) and notably absent from the Python client. DuckDB 2.0.0's Python client ships an appender that collects rows and writes them together in a single operation: import duckdb con = duckdb.connect() con.execute("CREATE TABLE duckdb_releases (version VARCHAR, codename VARCHAR);") with con.appender("duckdb_releases") as appender: appender.append_row("1.4", "Andium") appender.append_rows([("1.5", "Variegata"), ("2.0", "Cyanoptera")]) print(con.execute("FROM duckdb_releases").fetchall()) [('1.4', 'Andium'), ('1.5', 'Variegata'), ('2.0', 'Cyanoptera')] The with block flushes the buffered rows when it exi

entries.summary: The DuckDB team is happy to announce that today we're releasing DuckDB version 2.0.0 LTS, codenamed “Cinnamon Teal” (Spatula cyanoptera).
entries.text: Update DuckDB 2.0.0 packed so many features that we published a followup blog post titled “Gems of DuckDB 2.0.0”. We are proud to release DuckDB 2.0.0, codenamed “Cinnamon Teal” after the Spatula cyanoptera, a strikingly reddish-brown duck found in the western Americas. While DuckDB 1.0 was all about stability and backward compatibility, DuckDB 2.0 is above all a feature release. In this blog post, we summarize the highlights and then walk through the breaking changes and how to migrate. We showcased many of the new features in “A Preview of DuckDB v2.0”, which covers each one in more depth. For the complete release notes, see the release page on GitHub. Tip To install the new version, please visit the installation page. With this release, there are currently three DuckDB lines available. DuckDB 2.0 is a long-term support (LTS) release with support until at least October 2027. The previous LTS release, version 1.4, is still supported until November 17, 2026. To ensure a smooth transition and allow sufficient time for testing, we extended the support period of DuckDB 1.5 until March 2027, effectively also turning it into an LTS release. For details, see the release calendar. To find your way around the documentation for all of the new features, we also published a “What's New in the Docs for 2.0” page that links each feature below to its documentation. entries.summary: JSON often arrives as a text column inside a table, not as a file. In this post, we infer a schema from such a column, adjust it, and turn the column into typed columns, without first writing the data to a file.
entries.text: DuckDB's read_json turns JSON files into tables. It reads through part of the data to work out a schema, then gives you typed columns. However, a lot of JSON does not come as files. It comes as a text column: event payloads in a Postgres table, API responses stored by an ingestion job, a metadata column in a CSV export. People regularly ask how to get the read_json treatment for such a column, and one workaround that comes up is to COPY the column to a file and read the file back. You do not need the round trip. In this post, we get the same result directly in SQL. The Data Here is a small table of events, with the payload stored as VARCHAR: CREATE TABLE events (id INTEGER, payload VARCHAR); INSERT INTO events VALUES (1, '{"user": {"id": 17, "country": "NL"}, "action": "click", "ts": "2026-10-01 10:00:00"}'), (2, '{"user": {"id": 23, "country": "BE"}, "action": "view", "ts": "2026-10-01 10:00:05", "duration_ms": 1200}'), (3, '{"user": {"id": 17}, "action": "purchase", "ts": "2026-10-01 10:02:11", "items": [{"sku": "A-1", "qty": 2}, {"sku": "B-7", "qty": 1}]}'); Like most real payloads, the objects do not all have the same keys. Only the second event has a duration_ms, only the third has items, and the third has no country. Picking Out a Few Fields If you only need a handful of fields, the JSON extraction operators are enough. -> returns JSON and ->> returns VARCHAR. Both accept a key name or a JSON path: SELECT id, payload ->> '$.user.country' AS country, payload ->> 'action'
entries.title: From JSON Strings to Typed Columns
